headline: Cresco Labs grows sales 5% as discounts deepen and tax bill shrinks
dek: Cresco Labs posted $172.8 million in third-quarter revenue and $26.1 million in operating cash flow as discounts rose to 32.4% of gross sales.
key_points: Cresco Labs' third-quarter revenue rose about 5% from a year earlier to $172.8 million, flat against the second quarter, with retail now 70% of sales.
Gross margin fell to 46.0% from 50.2% in the second quarter as discounts climbed to 32.4% of gross revenue, and the company swung to a $14.5 million net loss.
Rescheduling has cut Cresco's tax bill: nine-month income tax expense was $5.0 million against $42.8 million a year earlier, as medical sales escape Section 280E from 22 April.
Shareholders approved a new Delaware parent company on 30 October, the groundwork for a future US listing with no exchange or date named yet.
body: Cresco Labs, the Chicago-based multi-state operator, reported third-quarter revenue of $172.8 million on 6 November, up about 5% from $164.9 million a year earlier but essentially unchanged from the $173.3 million it booked in the second quarter. Adjusted EBITDA came in at $34.9 million, a 20.2% margin, down from $39.8 million a year ago.

The headline numbers hide two forces pulling in opposite directions. Price pressure is eating into margins, with discounts now worth almost a third of gross sales. At the same time, the federal move of medical marijuana into Schedule III has sharply cut what Cresco owes in tax, and the company is quietly rebuilding its corporate structure for an eventual listing on a US exchange.
## The numbers

Cresco's GAAP gross margin fell to 46.0%, from 50.2% in the second quarter and 48.1% in the same quarter of 2025, according to its quarterly filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Gross profit was $79.5 million. Operating expenses rose: selling, general and administrative costs reached $57.7 million, or 33.4% of revenue, which the company attributes partly to one-off costs tied to acquisitions, preparing for an uplisting and federal reform work.

The bottom line swung to a $14.5 million net loss, after net income of $15.4 million in the second quarter. Income tax expense of $9.7 million was a large part of that swing. Cash generation held up better: operating cash flow was $26.1 million and free cash flow $21.2 million, roughly 61% of adjusted EBITDA.

The balance sheet carries $454 million of long-term notes and loans against $76 million of cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash. The largest piece is a $325 million senior secured term loan at 12.5% that runs to August 2030. Cresco also drew $28.4 million of a $50 million revolving credit line it opened in June.
## Discounts and the retail shift

The most telling figure sits in the management discussion: sales discounts were 32.4% of gross revenue in the quarter, up from 28.7% a year earlier. That is the price war in a single number. It means Cresco is giving away more of its sticker price to move product, and it explains why revenue growth did not reach the gross profit line.

The mix of the business is also changing. Retail made up 70% of revenue in the quarter against 64.2% a year earlier, while wholesale fell to 30% from 35.8%. By MetaFlora's arithmetic from those shares, retail revenue rose to roughly $121 million from about $106 million, while wholesale fell to roughly $52 million from about $59 million. Part of the retail gain is bought: on 1 September Cresco closed its acquisition of PharmaCann Penn, which runs nine medical dispensaries in Pennsylvania, for total consideration of $46.9 million. As of 6 November the company had 89 open dispensaries, including six partner locations, and 13 cultivation and production sites across eight states.
> Cresco is selling more through its own stores and earning less on each sale; the tax relief is what keeps the gap from showing.
## What rescheduling is already worth

The clearest early evidence of what Schedule III means for an operator is in Cresco's tax lines. Since 22 April, the filing says, costs tied to medical cannabis operations are deductible, because state-licensed medical marijuana moved to Schedule III under the April order and out of the reach of Section 280E. Adult-use operations remain caught by 280E.

The effect is visible in the totals. Income tax expense for the first nine months of 2026 was $5.0 million, against $42.8 million in the same period of 2025. Part of the gap reflects a catch-up adjustment Cresco made to its second-quarter provision to reflect the April effective date. The company says it is still waiting for guidance on whether the medical change applies retroactively, and it continues to treat adult-use tax positions as uncertain for 2026.
CEO Charlie Bachtell kept expectations in check. The company said it plans for the business it has, adding that "we do not build our plan around reform timelines."
## Preparing for a US listing

On 30 October shareholders approved three special resolutions with more than 94% support. They create a new parent company that would become the listed entity, move its domicile from British Columbia to Delaware, and extend the sunset on multiple voting shares from the first to the third anniversary of a US listing. Cresco says the aim is to simplify its capital structure before it taps US capital markets. It has not named an exchange or a date, and the change still has legal and regulatory steps to clear.

That matters because US multi-state operators like Cresco have traded over the counter and in Canada rather than on a major US exchange, and a Delaware parent is a prerequisite for changing that, not a ticket. The broader Schedule III question, now in the hands of a DEA administrative law judge, will shape whether an uplisting becomes possible for an operator with large adult-use sales.
## How it compares

Cresco's quarter looks modest next to its larger rivals. Curaleaf, which reported on 3 November, grew revenue 10.9% to $352.7 million with a 48.3% gross margin and a 22.0% adjusted EBITDA margin, though it too saw margins contract. Green Thumb, as we reported on 6 November, grew revenue 11.3% to $324.4 million.

On leverage, a rough MetaFlora calculation puts Cresco's net debt (debt less cash) at about 2.7 times its annualised third-quarter adjusted EBITDA, against roughly 1.7 times for Curaleaf on the same basis, using Curaleaf's $636.9 million of debt and $104.9 million of cash. These are simple ratios, not covenant measures, but they show why cash generation and the cost of that 12.5% term loan matter so much to Cresco's equity story.
## What to watch

Three things will set Cresco's next few quarters. First, whether discounting stabilises: another rise above 32.4% of gross sales would signal that price compression in its core markets is not over. Second, the federal timetable, from the DEA judge's recommendation on broader rescheduling to any IRS guidance on retroactive 280E relief, which could change the tax picture again. Third, the next step of the restructuring, including any filing that names an exchange. Cresco gave no fourth-quarter guidance in its release.
